name: Ivan Turgenev
teaser: The most European of the great Russians — elegant, melancholic, precise. Fathers and Sons gave the word 'nihilist' to the world, and his Sportsman's Sketches helped end serfdom.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Fathers and Sons, where Bazarov arrives with his sleeves rolled up and his opinions ready. Notice how Turgenev stages the clash of generations without taking sides. Write what nihilism meant in 1862 and what it means now.

name: Nikolai Gogol
teaser: The Ukrainian-born Russian genius of the grotesque. Dead Souls, The Overcoat, and The Nose turned Russian bureaucracy into surreal comedy that still stings — and made every writer after him measure themselves against him.

exploreAction.instruction: Read The Overcoat. Notice how Akaky Akakievich's whole life narrows to one coat, then the story turns fantastical. Write how Gogol makes us laugh at a clerk and then grieve for him — and what the ghost at the end is really doing.

name: Alexander Pushkin
teaser: The founding poet of Russian literature, who died in a duel at 37. Eugene Onegin invented the Russian novel in verse, and his tales made the language sing. Everything Russian literary starts at his door.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Eugene Onegin. Notice how Pushkin's narrator keeps interrupting the story with asides, jokes, and footnotes. Write how the 'Onegin stanza' creates a chatty, intimate voice that made Russian poetry feel newly alive.

name: Mikhail Lermontov
teaser: The Romantic poet and novelist who died at 27 in a duel he chose. A Hero of Our Time gave literature its first 'superfluous man' — Pechorin, bored, brilliant, and dangerous to everyone he meets.

exploreAction.targetName: A Hero of Our Time, Bela
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first story, Bela. Notice how the novel arrives at Pechorin through other people's accounts before he speaks. Write how Lermontov builds the portrait of a man who ruins others partly out of boredom with himself.

name: Boris Pasternak
teaser: Russian poet and novelist of Doctor Zhivago — a love story across revolution and war that got him the Nobel he was forced to refuse. His poetry moves with the force of weather and history.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Doctor Zhivago, where the young Yuri sees his mother buried in a snow-covered field. Notice how Pasternak ties private grief to the coming storm of history. Write how the novel treats the individual against the collective.

name: Anna Akhmatova
teaser: Russia's great poet of witness and loss. Requiem, written in secret about the Stalinist terror, stands among the century's most harrowing poems — a mother's voice speaking for millions of silent women.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Requiem, where Akhmatova waits in prison lines with the other women. Notice how the personal and the national fuse. Write what it means to 'speak for' those who cannot, and what courage her spare lines carry.

name: Marina Tsvetaeva
teaser: The Russian poet of explosive, irregular genius — diction that breaks syntax to say what it must. She lived in exile and poverty, and her letters and poems burn with intensity that later poets still feed on.

exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Tsvetaeva's poems. Notice how her punctuation and line breaks create urgency. Write how her style differs from more 'finished' poets, and what kind of truth demands broken syntax.

name: Osip Mandelstam
teaser: The Russian poet of classical clarity and terrible courage — he died in the camps after writing a poem against Stalin. His poetry balances stone-hard precision with deep musicality.

exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Mandelstam's poems, including one from the Voronezh notebooks. Notice how images of stone, water, and breath recur. Write how a poet composes when every word is dangerous, and what clarity means under threat.

name: Andrei Platonov
teaser: The strangest of Russian modernists — a Soviet writer whose skewed, tender, bureaucratic prose revealed the human wreckage of utopia. The Foundation Pit and Chevengur are bleak and holy books.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Foundation Pit. Notice how Platonov's workers dig with devotion while the language goes slightly wrong, like a badly translated dream. Write how his broken official prose mocks and mourns the project at once.

name: Isaac Babel
teaser: The Odessa-born writer of Red Cavalry — short, brutal, lyrical stories set in the Polish campaign — and of the Jewish gangsters of Odessa. He wrote slowly, perfectly, and was executed in 1940.

exploreAction.targetName: Red Cavalry, a cluster of stories
exploreAction.instruction: Read three stories from Red Cavalry. Notice how Babel compresses violence and beauty into a page — a field, a corpse, a sunset. Write how a writer of Jewish Odessa rode with Cossacks and looked at them with both awe and grief.

name: Yevgeny Zamyatin
teaser: The Russian engineer who wrote We, the dystopia that taught Orwell and Huxley their blueprints — a glass city of numbers and scheduled happiness. He saw the totalitarian future coming and said so in 1924.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the first 'records' of We. Notice how the narrator writes in numbered diary entries and calls himself D-503. Write how the language of the state colonizes even private feeling, and why the story remains so prophetic.

name: Stanisław Lem
teaser: The Polish science-fiction philosopher. Solaris and His Master's Voice ask whether we can ever understand an alien mind — and our own. He made sci-fi a laboratory for epistemology and wit.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Solaris. Notice how Lem's ocean-planet resists interpretation, and how the scientists project their own guilt onto it. Write what the novel suggests about the limits of knowledge and the loneliness of contact.

name: Czesław Miłosz
teaser: The Polish poet of witness and exile, who lived through the Nazi occupation of Warsaw and later taught in California. His poetry asks how one speaks after catastrophe — and his Nobel speech became a moral landmark.

exploreAction.targetName: Miłosz, poems from the war years
exploreAction.instruction: Read poems like A Poor Christian Looks at the Ghetto and Campo dei Fiori. Notice how Miłosz keeps turning from the event to the question of who tells it. Write what it means for poetry to 'witness' without being consumed.

name: Ivan Goncharov
teaser: The Russian novelist who gave the world Oblomov — the man who cannot get out of bed. A comic masterpiece of inertia, and one of the sharpest portraits of a soul in retreat from life.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Oblomov, where the hero stays on his sofa through every visitor's appeal. Notice how Goncharov makes inaction hilarious and strangely moving. Write what Oblomov's refusal means — laziness, protest, or fear?

name: Varlam Shalamov
teaser: The Russian writer who survived seventeen years in the Kolyma labor camps and spent his life writing Kolyma Tales — short, unsparing stories that refuse all comfort and nearly all metaphor.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one story from Kolyma Tales. Notice how Shalamov reports the camps without sentiment — frostbite, bread, the logic of survival. Write why he said prose must be 'cold' and what that coldness preserves.

name: Mikhail Sholokhov
teaser: The Cossack novelist of And Quiet Flows the Don — an epic of revolution told through one family's river of blood and love. He won the Nobel and remains Russia's most monumental storyteller of the civil war.

exploreAction.targetName: And Quiet Flows the Don, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of the epic, where the river and the village are introduced through the Melekhov family. Notice how Sholokhov grounds vast history in one household. Write how the Don itself becomes a character.

name: Andrey Bely
teaser: The Russian symbolist whose novel Petersburg is a prose symphony of the city — a cubist, ticking, hallucinated Petersburg on the eve of revolution. Nabokov ranked it among the greatest novels of the century.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Petersburg. Notice how the city is described in fragments, rhythms, and strange geometries. Write how the prose itself performs the nervous energy of the revolution it narrates.

name: Sławomir Mrożek
teaser: The Polish playwright and cartoonist of the absurd. His short stories and dramas, like Tango, use surreal logic to expose totalitarian habits — funny, bleak, and devastatingly precise.

exploreAction.instruction: Read three of Mrożek's very short stories. Notice how each begins with a plausible situation that tilts into the absurd. Write how comedy becomes a way of telling the truth about power that plain description cannot reach.

name: Aleksandar Hemon
teaser: The Bosnian-American novelist stranded in Chicago by the siege of Sarajevo, who learned English and wrote The Question of Bruno and The Lazarus Project — memory, displacement, and history braided together.

exploreAction.targetName: The Question of Bruno, a story
exploreAction.instruction: Read a story from The Question of Bruno. Notice how Hemon scrambles chronology, genre, and voice. Write how the experience of exile shapes a writer's relationship to language — what does it mean to be 'born again' into English?

name: Andrey Kurkov
teaser: The Ukrainian novelist of the absurd and the everyday — Death and the Penguin follows a writer who keeps a penguin named Misha in post-Soviet Kyiv. His books read like black comedies of survival.

exploreAction.targetName: Death and the Penguin, opening chapters
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of Death and the Penguin. Notice how Viktor's life — obituaries for the living, a penguin for company — is both surreal and perfectly believable. Write how the penguin becomes a mirror of its owner's isolation.

name: Serhiy Zhadan
teaser: The Ukrainian poet and novelist of the east — Kharkiv's chronicler. Voroshilovgrad and The Orphanage mix punk energy, tenderness, and war; his poetry speaks for a generation living through upheaval.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Orphanage. Notice how Zhadan balances the surreal violence of war with precise domestic detail. Write how the novel treats the duty to protect one child while the world burns around you.

name: Mikhail Saltykov-Shchedrin
teaser: The great Russian satirist of the 19th century, whose The Golovlyov Family and The History of a Town flayed bureaucracy, serfdom, and hypocrisy with savage laughter. Dostoevsky called him a prophet.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening of The Golovlyov Family. Notice how Saltykov-Shchedrin's portrait of a decaying gentry family mixes farce and horror. Write how the novel's central figure, Iudushka, becomes a study in sanctimonious cruelty.
